Song about young girl who has survived five operations beats Barry Manilow in the charts A song written about a little girl who has survived five life-threatening operations is proving a huge success - even knocking Barry Manilow off the top of an easy-listening chart.

Kiahna's Song is about eight-year-old Kiahna Taylor-Brummell, daughter of publicans Neil Taylor and Kerry Brummell who run the Fox at Shipley pub near Pattingham.

Penned by Mr Taylor's friends, Andrew Ayres and Steph Burgess, from Stoke, the song has exceeded all expectations.

And now the people behind it are aiming for the top 40, with money raised going to Birmingham Children's Hospital.

The song celebrates the youngster's courage and determination and tells the story of a parent's anxious wait for their child to return from theatre and a critical operation.

Mr Taylor, 44, said he was overwhelmed with the success of the song, which can regularly be heard playing at the pub.

"It's gone really well and obviously all the money goes to the children's hospital.

"Andrew has come up with a beautiful song to depict an extremely emotional time in our lives and one that a lot of parents can sympathise with.

"It has tugged at a lot of heart strings and I'm hoping we can achieve the unthinkable and actually get into the official top 40.

"I know Kiahna's really excited about the possibility of being in the same chart as One Direction and Union J."

The two performers have themselves experienced their own young children being seriously ill.

Mr Ayres said he was shocked and delighted at how well Kiahna's Song had been received.

He added: "To knock Barry Manilow off the number one spot in any chart is something every musician dreams of, but the fact we're raising money for such an outstanding charity makes it even better.

"You never know, he might even download a copy himself."

The single is the latest in a number of fundraising ventures in aid of Kiahna and Birmingham Children's Hospital.

Football matches and quiz nights have been held at the Fox at Shipley, while Mr Taylor also completed a gruelling seven-day challenge earlier this year,which included running the Paris and London marathons and riding more than 400 miles to get to both events.

Mar'dy was awoken in the middle of night by a young Flora tugging on his toes. He stepped out of his tent to see the Flora gathered around a large bonfire. When they saw him they began to whistle and chant. It was the first of the Flora late night celebrations he had seen, they seemed to do them weekly, just party for an hour or two, chant in unison, beat drums and then go back to sleep. This time they were focussed on him.

One of the older flora stepped out in front of him: "Mar'dy Kist. Are you ready to be a pattern incarnate?"

"W-what does that entail exactly?"

"It is the highest honour, no Flora are worthy of it. To have the holy patterns upon your own flesh."

Figuring it was just a painting exercise, Mar'dy agreed. He felt less confident when they strapped him to a contraption to hold him still. First they brought a black oil. He had recognized it as Blackbark oil, it was a strong topical anesthetic with the unfortunate side effect of permanently turning your skin pitch black. They coated his entire body in it. Soon it was numb and his muscles were limp. He could not even utter a protest as he was drooling over himself.

Next came the master pattern carver. He was completely blind but he was known for making the greatest most symmetrical of all patterns. He held a small chip of obsidian. "Shit," Mar'dy thought. He tried to say "Please stop" but it came out as "Pleshhh Starrrrrp"

The old Flora must have heard it differently. "Mar'dy Kist the brave wants us to start!" The crowd roared in excitement. Defeated, Mar'dy let out a protestful "Aulllppp".

The master carver took his time and even though Mar'dy couldn't feel it or see it, he could see little shavings of black skin being thrown in the fire and blood covered hands moving his head and limbs around.

Then they brought out some gold dust. It was finely powder and placed in a little clay crucible. Heat in the fire until they glowed red. They placed this dust in the grooves the pattern carver made, and it instantly cauterized the skin. the gold powder diffused into the scar tissue of the grooves leaving them a dull gold colour against his now black skin. For the next few days as feeling came back to him, Saule filled in his administrative duties and told him stories to keep him company as he healed.
